doc.title: Jerome Richardson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996

title: Recording Midnight Oil and studio practice at Prestige
summary: Discussion of his album Midnight Oil with alto flute, its personnel, one-day sessions and Prestige's lack of promotion.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So a couple of years after you got here — we did find your — there you go with the alto flute.
Yeah. Let me see what was on that, yeah, “Midnight Oil.”
Notes by Ira Gitler. You had a nice band on that with Hank Jones and your friend Kenny Burrell.
Yeah. Jimmy Cleveland, Hank Jones, Kenny Burrell, Joe Benjamin and Charlie Persip on drums.
What was it like in the studio for an album like this? Did they give you a day, a couple of days?

In those days it was done in one day. You might get a double date out of it, but it was done all day long. I should have said — I said “Midnight Oil” — see I should have said “All Night Long.” Well there’s another one I did called “All Night Long” anyway. I should have tried to be different with the music on that.

Well it was a different approach. I was playing alto flute in some, harmonically it was a different approach. And it was what you might call esoteric. And it didn’t catch on very well because they couldn’t tell whether it was commercial or good jazz or one of those things.
It was in the cracks, right?

Right down the middle you know. Although Prestige wasn’t doing anything about advertising and promoting no one’s record at that time. I used to say they used to go up on the Empire State Building and throw all the records off, and the one that ended up on the edge on the ground, that’s the one they’d do something with. So you know they didn’t do anything with anything, you know.
